Every eight hours, SpaceX publishes where each of about eleven thousand Starlink satellites will be for the next three days, and how sure it is. Eight hours later that set is gone, replaced by the next one. Ephemera keeps them, and measures what the public catalogue can see.

The files carry a full position and velocity uncertainty every sixty seconds, read from the feed on 30 August 2026. Starlink is the only operator with public covariance; other operators enter via CelesTrak SupGP without covariance.

What the public catalogue can see

Headline figures from cycle ac2fb0c90f26, first seen 2026-11-12 05:13 UTC, scored 2026-11-12 05:58 UTC against the public catalogue snapshot fetched 2026-11-12 04:17 UTC (13,026 element sets).

At the first instant of each operator file, the public catalogue puts 76% of the scored Starlink satellites within 10 km of where the operator says they are. The middle satellite is 3.9 km away, with the public information a median of 10 hours old. Where the public information is two to three days old, the two predictions are about 63 km apart. Both sides are predictions, and most of that spread is planned trajectory changes the public catalogue cannot know about.

Everyone outside SpaceX sees Starlink through the public catalogue of orbital elements. Ephemera takes that public element set for each satellite, propagates it with SGP4, and compares it against the operator's own published trajectory for the same satellite at the same instants. The distance between the two is what this measures. It is not an error of the satellite, and it is not a statement about which side is right.

1 satellites (0.0%) are more than 1,000 km from the public prediction at publication, more than two minutes of flight along the orbit. For those the public element set is not on the operator's trajectory at all. Ephemera does not label any separation as a manoeuvre; that needs a detector this project has not built.

Feed health for this cycle. 11,192 of 11,192 operator files scored. 0 have no entry in the public catalogue. Nothing else was dropped. Public element sets were a mean of 13.5 h old when the snapshot was taken (median 10.9 h, 90th percentile 25.6 h, 1 over 72 h). Averaged over every comparison, which run out to three days into the operator file, element age is 48.5 h: the difference is the file's own prediction horizon, not catalogue staleness. Space-Track: 677 snapshots held, last fetched 2026-11-12 04:17 UTC with 13,026 element sets. Poller heartbeat coverage over the last 24 h: 100.0%.

The archive behind it

As of 2026-11-12 07:30 UTC. Poller: A (a datacentre host in the EU; the home poller was retired on 3 Oct 2026).

The operator side of every comparison comes from files this project caught before they were replaced. Each cycle is hashed file by file into one Merkle root, the root is stamped into the Bitcoin blockchain through OpenTimestamps, and the manifest plus ten files chosen by the root itself are pushed into the Wayback Machine so an independent copy exists that this project does not control.

As of 2026-11-12 07:30 UTC: 232 cycles, 231 complete with roots, 230 anchored in Bitcoin, 16 with a defect in the independent copy. Source bytes archived: 5,273 GB across 2,597,815 files as served. Stored gzipped as 2,168 GB, of which 28 GB is on the poller's disk and 2,140 GB exists only in cold object storage. Cadence holds, meaning a set served longer than nine hours while the poller watched: 20. A further 3 such intervals fell while the poller was down and are not counted as a hold. Poller heartbeat coverage over the last 24 hours: 100.0%. This project exists because SpaceX publishes the feed openly.

Check it yourself

None of this is worth anything if you have to take my word for it. Three things you can run right now, for cycle e3b1280f5578, the newest one with a Bitcoin attestation and a verified independent copy:

  1. Fetch the independent copy of the file list and hash it. SHA-256 e3b1280f5578a8568c41b688801e518d955bfb7d203c067391848a3437e149af. It arrives gzipped, so with curl use --compressed.
  2. Recompute which ten files were copied: int(sha256(root + ":" + k), 16) mod n, counting files from zero, for k = 0, 1, 2 and on, skipping repeats until there are ten.
  3. Download root.txt and root.txt.ots, then run ots verify root.txt.ots against a Bitcoin node: this root is in block 975480.

The full procedure, and what you cannot check from here yet.

Data, licence and citation

ledger.json carries every cycle, its root, its attestation, its witness state and every scored summary, as the JSON the pages are built from. The globe's per-cycle pack is at the newest cycle's pack (5.3 MB). The full per-comparison rows, about 140,000 per cycle, are available on request.

Code is MIT and the repository is public, including the propagation and the scoring behind every figure here. Figures derived by this project are intended for CC BY 4.0. The raw SpaceX files carry no stated licence; a written request went to SpaceX on 31 August 2026 and had received no answer by 30 September 2026, the thirty days it was given; the files are held as published and come down on request. Licence and citation in full.

Not here yet

74 days of archive is not a long record, and this page should not pretend otherwise. What is not running:

  • A second poller on a different machine in a different country.
  • The self-consistency scoreboard, prediction against later prediction.
  • The manoeuvre census: three differently defined counts side by side, never a ratio.
  • Other constellations, via CelesTrak SupGP without covariance.
  • A restore drill from cold storage.

Operator ephemerides are predictions, not observations. Starlink is the only operator with public covariance; other operators enter via CelesTrak SupGP without covariance. Public GP data is too noisy to test sub-metre covariance; the self-consistency scoreboard measures prediction-versus-later-prediction. That scoreboard is not built yet. Inputs are archived by this project and witnessed by OpenTimestamps and the Wayback Machine; they are not re-fetchable from the source after one cycle. Gapped or lost items are printed, never hidden.
